summary: Plant reproduction for ages 12-13: flower structure, wind vs insect pollination as adaptations, pollination vs fertilisation, seed/fruit formation, and seed dispersal including a quantitative dispersal investigation. The teaching centres on framing pollination and dispersal adaptations as cause-and-effect arguments about reproductive success (including that pollination is an incidental by-product of pollinator behaviour the flower exploits, not deliberate insect intent), keeping pollination (pollen transfer) and fertilisation (gamete fusion) clearly distinct, and backing dispersal claims with measured data.
misconceptions: Conflating pollination with fertilisation — treating the arrival of pollen on the stigma as the moment a seed is made, rather than a separate later fusion after the pollen tube grows.
Thinking all flowers are brightly coloured and scented — wind-pollinated flowers are typically dull, scentless and nectarless, which pupils often overlook.
Believing the fruit and the seed are the same thing — the seed develops from the fertilised ovule; the fruit develops from the ovary around it and aids dispersal.
Assuming pollination and dispersal serve the same purpose — pollination brings gametes together; dispersal spreads offspring away from the parent to reduce competition.
Thinking bees intend to pollinate — pollination is an incidental consequence of insects seeking nectar; the plant's structures exploit that behaviour (a cause-and-effect point central to MS-LS1-4).

activities.title: Dissect and label a real flower
steps: Examine a real flower (or a high-fidelity model if a real one is unavailable) and locate each structure by eye and, where possible, by touch.
Find the pollen on the anthers and feel the sticky stigma before any labels are given.
Label the main parts: sepals, petals, stamen (anther + filament), carpel (stigma + style + ovary containing ovules).
Open or drill into the carpel to find the hidden ovules, and name each part's job alongside its name.
activities.insight: A flower's parts are physical structures with specific functions. Examining or handling a real flower (or model) makes those structures concrete, though a clear 2D cross-section can also support labelling; neither is a universal requirement. The goal is to be able to reason later about how each structure affects reproductive success.

activities.title: Two flowers, one problem: wind vs insect pollination
steps: Compare side by side an insect-pollinated bloom (bright scented petals, nectar, sticky/spiky pollen) and a wind-pollinated grass flower (small dull flowers, no scent or nectar, feathery stigmas, light abundant pollen).
Build a comparison table: for each feature, state its function and how it raises the chance of pollen reaching another flower.

For each adaptation, answer 'why does this raise the plant's chance of making seeds?' as an explicit cause→effect statement (e.g. 'bright petals cause more insect visits, which raises the chance of pollination').
Explain why an insect visiting a flower ends up transferring pollen to another flower even though it is only seeking food (nectar, or pollen to eat), not trying to pollinate.
activities.insight: Two very different-looking flowers are solving the same problem (getting pollen to another flower) in two ways: one attracts insects with colour and nectar, the other releases clouds of light pollen to the wind. Each feature is an adaptation whose cause→effect link to reproductive success can be argued. Crucially, insects do not set out to pollinate — pollination is an incidental consequence of food-seeking (nectar and/or pollen) that the flower's structures exploit.

activities.title: Trace the journey: pollination to dispersal
steps: Sequence the stages: pollen lands on stigma → pollen tube grows down the style → fertilises the ovule → ovule becomes seed, ovary becomes fruit → seed is dispersed.

State in your own words how pollination differs from fertilisation: pollination is the TRANSFER of pollen from anther to stigma; fertilisation is the later fusion of gamete nuclei after the pollen tube grows down.

Identify which part becomes the seed (the fertilised ovule) and which becomes the fruit (the ovary around it), and what the petals do in insect-pollinated flowers (attract pollinators, then usually wither and fall away).

Explain how pollination and dispersal serve different purposes: pollination delivers pollen (which carries the male gametes) to the stigma so that fertilisation can follow; dispersal spreads offspring away from the parent to reduce competition and reach new places to grow.
activities.insight: Making a seed is a sequence of distinct steps, not a single moment. Pollination and fertilisation are separate events, and seed and fruit develop from different structures and serve a different purpose from dispersal.

activities.title: Quantitative dispersal investigation
steps: Build winged 'helicopter' paper seeds of varying wing size.

Drop them from a fixed height and measure fall-time for each design (longer fall-time means more time for wind to carry the seed). If measuring dispersal distance, use a steady sideways airflow (e.g. a fan on a fixed setting at a fixed position), because a drop in still air gives little sideways travel. Keep the paper type and any added mass (e.g. one paper clip) the same so that only wing size changes, and repeat each drop.

Record the data (using means of repeats), plot fall-time or distance against wing area, and argue from the plot which wing design is likely to disperse best and why, noting that fall-time stands in for how far wind could carry the seed and that the trend may not keep rising for very large wings.
Describe at least two dispersal mechanisms from the wider set (winged/wind, hooked or edible/animal, explosive, water) and explain how each works.
activities.insight: Dispersal adaptations can be investigated empirically: measured data about wing size and fall-time/distance support an evidence-based argument about which structures disperse seeds most effectively.

activities.title: Defend your claim: botanist argument
steps: Take the role of a botanist and justify a pollination or dispersal claim when probed (e.g. 'What evidence shows bright petals raise reproductive success?').
Respond to follow-up challenges by citing specific adaptations or measured data (ideally the dispersal data you collected).
Construct a short spoken or written argument linking a structure to its effect on reproductive success.
activities.insight: Scientific claims about adaptations must be backed by evidence and reasoning; practising the back-and-forth of justification can strengthen the argument-from-evidence skill.

checkQuestion: A bee visits a flower and pollen sticks to it, then it flies to another flower where the pollen rubs off. People often say the second flower is 'fertilised' the moment the pollen lands. Is that right? Explain what pollination is and whether it's the same as fertilisation.
checkAnswer: No — pollination is only the TRANSFER of pollen from the stamen (anther) to the stigma; fertilisation happens afterwards, when the male cell from the pollen travels down to join the female ovule in the ovary. Pollination must happen first, but they are two separate steps, and a seed forms only after fertilisation.
